subject: Computer Networking
title: WannaCry Ransomware (2017)
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on WannaCry Ransomware (2017).

hook.text: In May 2017, a worm infected 200,000 computers across 150 countries in one day. Hospitals turned away patients.

buildup.text: WannaCry used EternalBlue, an NSA exploit leaked by hackers. It targeted unpatched Windows systems.

discovery.text: It spread automatically across networks. No click needed — just an open port was enough to get infected.

twist.text: A researcher accidentally stopped it by registering a domain in the code — a kill switch nobody expected.

climax.text: The UK's NHS was hit hard. Surgeries were cancelled. Global damage exceeded $4 billion.

punchline.text: A leaked spy tool became the world's most destructive worm.

quiz.question: How was WannaCry accidentally stopped?
options: A researcher registered a domain that acted as a kill switch
Antivirus software detected it within minutes
Microsoft released an emergency patch before it spread

details.summary: WannaCry ransomware spread through a leaked NSA exploit called EternalBlue in May 2017, infecting over 200,000 computers across 150 countries in days. It crippled the UK's National Health Service, Telefonica, and FedEx.
details.whyItMatters: WannaCry showed that government-hoarded exploits become weapons when leaked. It demonstrated that unpatched systems across critical infrastructure create global vulnerability.
takeaways: WannaCry used a leaked NSA exploit called EternalBlue
Over 200,000 computers in 150 countries were infected
A researcher's accidental kill switch discovery stopped it

faq.question: How did a researcher accidentally stop WannaCry?
faq.answer: Marcus Hutchins noticed WannaCry checked if a specific domain name was registered. He registered it for a few dollars, which activated a kill switch the malware authors had built in. The worm stopped spreading to new machines as soon as the domain went live.

faq.question: Why were so many systems vulnerable to WannaCry?
faq.answer: Microsoft had released a patch for the EternalBlue vulnerability two months before WannaCry. Many organizations, including the NHS, had not applied the patch. Legacy Windows XP systems were especially vulnerable because they were officially unsupported.
